phase1.intro:
Okay, first things first — what even IS Java?

I'm basically running a workshop where everything I build uses the same language. James Gosling and his team created it back in 1995 at Sun Microsystems, and their whole obsession was one rule: whatever you build here should work everywhere, not just on the machine that built it.

So — where do you want to start?

topics.buttonText: How does my code run on any computer?
dialogue:
That rule I mentioned has a name — [[term:WORA]]: Write Once, Run Anywhere.

Here's how it actually works: you write your code, and instead of turning it directly into instructions for YOUR specific computer, it gets compiled into something called [[term:bytecode]] — a kind of universal blueprint.

Then any machine with a [[term:JVM]] (Java Virtual Machine) installed can read that blueprint and run it — whether it's Windows, Mac, Linux, or, I promise I'm not exaggerating, an actual internet-connected fridge somewhere.

The JVM is what makes [[term:platform independence]] possible. One blueprint, any machine.

stickyNote.flavor: 🌍 the promise that your code isn't picky about computers
stickyNote.definition: Write Once, Run Anywhere — Java compiles to bytecode, which any JVM can run regardless of operating system.

topics.buttonText: Why does Java call everything an object?
dialogue:
I build with [[key:objects, not just instructions]].

Almost everything you'll write with me is a blueprint — we call it a [[term:class]] — for some kind of object. A BankAccount, a Shape, a Person. You design the blueprint once, then make as many objects from it as you want.

Think of it like a cookie cutter. The class is the cutter; the objects are the cookies. Same shape, different dough. This blueprint-first way of thinking is called [[term:Object-Oriented Programming]], and it's the backbone of how Java works — and honestly, how most modern languages think now.

stickyNote.flavor: 🍪 classes are cookie cutters, objects are the cookies
stickyNote.definition: A programming style where you define classes (blueprints) and create objects from them. Java is built around this idea from the ground up.

topics.buttonText: Why does Java make me declare variable types?
dialogue:
I label everything before I use it. Java is [[term:strongly typed]] — it wants to know a variable's type upfront, before you're allowed to use it.

[[warn:Feels strict at first]]. It really does. But it's actually Java double-checking your work before you get too far in.

If you try to put a word where a number goes, Java catches it immediately — not after you've already run the program and confused a user. The compiler is just a very thorough editor who won't let you submit a draft with obvious errors.

stickyNote.flavor: 🏷️ Java reads the label before opening the box
stickyNote.definition: Every variable must have a declared type. Java checks types at compile time, catching type mismatches before the program ever runs.

topics.buttonText: Who cleans up memory after I'm done?
dialogue:
This one's my favorite, because the answer is: not you.

Java has [[term:garbage collection]]. Once you're done using something — a variable, an object, whatever — you just stop using it. The JVM quietly figures out that nothing's referring to it anymore, and clears it out of memory for you.

In older languages like C, forgetting to clean up your memory yourself was one of the most common ways programs went wrong. Java just... removed that whole category of mistake. [[key:You focus on what to build. The JVM handles the cleanup.]]

stickyNote.flavor: 🗑️ the JVM is your silent cleanup crew
stickyNote.definition: Automatic memory management — the JVM detects objects that are no longer referenced and reclaims their memory, so you don't have to.

phase1.openingDialogue: Welcome to the workshop~ First things first: let's talk about what we're actually building with. ☕

phase2.explanation: Nothing to break yet — we haven't built anything! Once we write our first real program together in the next lesson, this is exactly where I'll show you how it breaks, and more importantly, how you fix it. Consider this the calm before a very useful storm~
phase2.openingDialogue: No bugs to squash just yet — patience, we're getting there~

phase3.openingDialogue: Nothing to build with your own hands yet either — next lesson, I promise. For now, let's just check what stuck.

mcq.question:
Quick check before we start building — which of these is actually true about Java?

A) Your compiled program only runs on the machine that compiled it
B) Java uses raw pointers like C or C++
C) Write Once, Run Anywhere — the same bytecode runs on any machine with a JVM
D) You have to manually free memory yourself

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: Java wasn't always called Java! Gosling's team first called the project "Oak," after a tree outside his office. When it turned out another company already had "Oak" trademarked, the team went looking for a new name during a coffee run — and "Java," slang for coffee, stuck. That's also why the logo is a steaming coffee cup. Every time you see that cup icon, that's a coffee run that changed programming history.
phase5.openingDialogue: Before you go — one more thing I think you'll like~
